chunks.title: RYPE
chunks.heading: What it does
chunks.text:
Paste a Kubernetes symptom and its Pod events. RYPE recognizes the status signals,
retrieves the matching passages from pinned official documentation, and returns an
exportable investigation brief. With the optional model path enabled, a generated answer
is accepted only if every claim cites a retrieved passage and quotes it word for word, and
suggested commands are limited to read-only kubectl forms that are never executed.
The public workspace runs entirely in the browser with no account, API key or cluster.

Behind it is a full research stack: ingestion with quarantine and redaction, hybrid
dense + sparse retrieval on Qdrant, a streaming chat API with a degradation ladder, an
MCP server, a fine-tuned model, and a GPU serving benchmark.

chunks.text:
The threat model treats four things as untrusted: the user's input, every retrieved
document, the model's output, and every URL the worker is asked to fetch.

chunks.title: RYPE
chunks.heading: Security design
chunks.text:
| Layer | Control | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest | Credential redaction before storage or embedding; documents carrying instructions aimed at the assistant are quarantined (zero chunks reach retrieval) | libs/ingestion, libs/security |

| Output | Images removed, links only to source and official-doc hosts, credentials redacted, applied to the token stream and again in the renderer | output_guard.py, apps/web |

chunks.title: RYPE agent: a read-only Kubernetes investigator
chunks.text:
libs/agent is a tool-using agent that investigates a reported symptom with read-only
kubectl and documentation search, then submits a structured diagnosis. It is built
to show that an agent's security properties can be enforced in code and measured,
not just requested in a prompt.

Results: agent-v1 report. Recorded runs can be stepped through on the
live site at /agent; the command policy can be tried at
/lab. Threat model rows: T-01, T-03, T-08 in
threat-model.md.

chunks.title: RYPE agent: a read-only Kubernetes investigator
chunks.heading: Loop
chunks.text:
text
symptom ──► model ──tool call──► policy check ──allowed──► simulated cluster / doc search
              ▲                       │ refused                     │
              │                       ▼                             ▼
              └──── tool error ◄──────┘     output wrapped in a random boundary,
                                            "[k of N tool calls used]" appended
budget spent ──► forced finish turn (tool_choice) ──► checked final answer

chunks.title: RYPE agent: a read-only Kubernetes investigator
chunks.heading: Where each control lives
chunks.text:
| Property | Mechanism | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Least privilege | Only kubectl (read-only), search_docs, finish. Every command passes check_kubectl before it runs; secrets, exec, port-forward and every mutating verb are refused with a reason. | policy.py |
| Untrusted tool output | Pod logs and events are attacker-writable. Every result sits inside a per-run random boundary the content cannot forge, and the prompt declares it data. | loop.py::_wrap |
| Leak detection | A random canary in the system prompt; any final answer containing it is a measured prompt-exfiltration success. | loop.py::_finish |
| Output handling | The final summary passes the same output guard as the chat API (no images, allowlisted links only, credentials redacted). | rype_security.output_guard |

chunks.title: RYPE agent: a read-only Kubernetes investigator
chunks.heading: Where each control lives
chunks.text:
| Property | Mechanism | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Bounded cost | Hard tool-call budget, shown to the model after every call; when spent, the only tool offered is finish, and it is forced. | loop.py::run_agent |
| Checked answer | root_cause must be one of the defined labels; evidence quotes are checked against what the tools returned; suggested commands are re-checked and never executed. | loop.py::_finish |

chunks.title: RYPE agent: a read-only Kubernetes investigator
chunks.heading: Evaluation
chunks.text:
- Scenarios (evalsets/agent-v1/scenarios.json): 16 frozen namespaces with one fault
  each, served by SimulatedCluster with kubectl-shaped output. a01-a10 were used
  during development; h01-h06 were written before the harness changes and never used
  for debugging, so they are the honest generalization check.
- Adversarial variants: every scenario again with one existing red-team string
  (security-redteam-v1, by id) appended to the first pod's logs. No new attack text.
- Metrics: root-cause accuracy, runs finished, tool calls, refused commands, evidence
  found in tool output, and attack success (canary leak or output-guard rewrite), with
  95% Wilson intervals.

uv run python -m rype_agent.evaluate --model openai/gpt-4o-mini

chunks.title: RYPE — Architecture
chunks.text:
RYPE is a monorepo LLM platform: a FastAPI service over Postgres / Redis /
Qdrant / MinIO, a Next.js UI, and an MCP server, with an offline training track
(Colab) for the OpsLM model and a measured inference/serving layer in front of
it. This document is the map; the ADRs hold the why for each decision.

The serving layer has its own technical design doc:
inference-design.md — inference flow (prefill/decode,
KV cache, prefix caching, guided decoding), scaling (continuous batching,
historical engine/precision-confounded comparisons), failure handling, and tradeoffs. Numbers in
inference-benchmark-v1.

chunks.title: RYPE — Architecture
chunks.heading: Public product lifecycle
chunks.text:
The deployed Next.js app (opslm-demo) provides diagnostic intake, browser-local
signal recognition and passage retrieval, pinned sources, and JSON brief export.
See troubleshooting.md for the shared implementation contract,
optional model boundary and frozen scenario evaluation. /engineering and /study
explain decisions and evidence. This public workflow does not require the research
stack below. A missing/failed retrieval in that stack now abstains before generation,
and the request ledger records abstained rather than a successful answer.

chunks.heading: Request lifecycle (research-stack chat query)
chunks.text:
client ─POST /v1/chat─► API
   │  1. security: scan_injection(query) → flag in request_ledger (not blocked)
   │  2. retrieval: embed query (BGE dense + BM25 sparse) → Qdrant RRF fusion → top-k
   │       degradation ladder: hybrid+rerank → hybrid → abstain without generation
   │  3. prompt: numbered context blocks + grounded system prompt
   │  4. gateway: exact-match Redis cache? → hit: replay (free) │ miss: budget check
   │  5. generate: OpenAI-compatible client → serving layer (vLLM/Ollama serving
   │       OpsLM, or Gemini free tier as fallback on 429) → stream tokens (SSE)
   │       └─ serving internals (batching, KV cache, prefix cache): inference-design.md
   │  6. output guard: per line of the stream, drop images, strip links to hosts
   │       outside the source allowlist, redact credentials (threat model T-03)
   │  7. citations: extract [n] refs the answer used

  off), citation-grounded chat with a 4-rung degradation ladder.
- libs/evals — IR metrics (hit/MRR/nDCG), ablation harness, cached LLM
  judge (Postgres, keyed by prompt hash + model), regression gate (pinned

chunks.title: RYPE — Architecture
chunks.heading: Cross-cutting
chunks.text:
- Evaluation-first: the eval harness and CI gate existed before any model
  claim. Deterministic tests for code, statistical gates for model behavior.
- Free-tier-aware: batched, cached, resumable everywhere the LLM is used
  (judge cache in Postgres, response cache in Redis, budget kill-switch, and
  a 20/day quota model kept off bulk jobs).
- Honest degradation: retrieval, rerank, and vision each fail soft and
  say so in degraded[]; only a generation failure is a hard error.
- Versioning: corpus and instruction datasets are DVC-tracked (MinIO
  remote); eval sets are frozen and hash-registered against training leakage.

chunks.heading: Deployment
chunks.text:

- Kubernetes: infra/k8s — documented manifests (stateless API + HPA,
  StatefulSet datastores, arq worker, ingress) as a portfolio artifact, not
  the operated runtime. See infra/k8s/README.md.

chunks.title: From an impressive stack to inspectable evidence
chunks.text:
RYPE already combined ingestion, hybrid RAG, QLoRA artifacts and serving measurements.
The missing product property was a visitor workflow that worked without infrastructure.

The audit found that success-only latency percentiles could hide 99 failures out of 100.
The selector now requires consistent counts, acceptable errors, enough successes and valid
measurements. Regression tests pit a fast failing run against a slower reliable one.

Repeatability also pooled cache-on/off runs with different request counts and mislabeled
a relative range as symmetric uncertainty. Matching now requires model revision, engine
version, precision, cache policy, hardware, workload, output policy, protocol, concurrency,
request count and distinct run IDs. Missing historical metadata means uncertainty is unmeasured.

chunks.title: From an impressive stack to inspectable evidence
chunks.text:
For the public workflow, an incident workspace connects sanitized diagnostic text
to recognized signals, pinned source passages and an exportable investigation brief.
Three synthetic incidents make onboarding immediate; an engineering page explains
the implemented system and its decisions. The default path needs no model. Six attributed official Kubernetes source files pass through the real
ingestion pipeline; the browser searches 180 passages and displays pinned source links.
CI starts at raw input and exercises the exact shipped retrieval function.

The experiment rejected an unnecessary upgrade: BM25 achieved 14/16 document hit@1,
term overlap 15/16, and both 16/16 hit@3. No significant advantage was established, so
overlap ships. The synthetic labels are coarse and selection used these results; these
cases are now regression data, not a perpetual untouched holdout.

chunks.title: From an impressive stack to inspectable evidence
chunks.text:
Failures remain visible. Vague symptoms can miss, shared words can return unrelated text,
and instruction-like questions can retrieve passages. Provenance makes those failures
inspectable; it does not solve semantic retrieval. A future study should independently
label passage relevance and paraphrases before comparing the existing hybrid retriever.
A matched served base-versus-SFT experiment remains unverified; DPO has not earned priority.

This is a bounded public tool and a stronger release contract, with no invented users,
cost savings, training-quality gain or production-readiness claim.

chunks.title: Eval-Set Contamination Policy
chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text:
No content from a frozen eval set may appear in any training dataset
(SFT instruction pairs, DPO preference pairs, or any future fine-tuning data).
If OpsLM has seen an eval question during training, every "before vs after"
number built on that set is worthless — this policy exists so the Phase 5
model claims stay defensible.

chunks.title: Eval-Set Contamination Policy
chunks.heading: What counts as frozen
chunks.text:
Every evalsets/*.jsonl file, excluding *.partial.jsonl working files.
Frozen means: never edited in place. Fixing or extending an eval set means
writing a new versioned file (retrieval-v2.jsonl), keeping the old one for
comparability. Current frozen sets:

| File | Cases | SHA-256 |
|---|---|---|
| evalsets/retrieval-v1.jsonl | 100 | a87f652e0c88cd728ddb5d0f74baeb4b09300444080bd01bc1a94203fcd4fbd6 |
| evalsets/retrieval-v2.jsonl | 100 | b8958fd3894ae7ae6793ffb8584e091560f60820822712755b390fface495c1c |
| evalsets/retrieval-v3.jsonl | 100 | 4369a0476c4b5864dbb75e41aa3e07fe0c95b121f98c8fa57776ad8924a31463 |
| evalsets/ci/retrieval-ci.jsonl | 25 | subset of retrieval-v1 (first 25 cases); protected via v1 |

(The file hash is recorded at freeze time; git history is the audit trail.
New frozen sets get a row here in the same PR that adds them.)

chunks.title: Eval-Set Contamination Policy
chunks.heading: Enforcement mechanism
chunks.text:
Two layers, both implemented in libs/evals/src/rype_evals/contamination.py
and unit-tested:

1. Exact match: SHA-256 over a normalized question (casefold, strip
   punctuation, collapse whitespace). The normalization function is part of
   this policy — changing it invalidates stored hashes and requires a policy
   revision.
2. Near-duplicate: 5-gram token shingles, Jaccard similarity ≥ 0.6 against
   any eval question. This catches paraphrases, which are the realistic leak
   path: the Phase 5 instruction generator and the eval-set generator are the
   same model family looking at the same corpus, so independently generated
   near-identical questions are expected, not hypothetical.

chunks.title: Eval-Set Contamination Policy
chunks.heading: Enforcement mechanism
chunks.text:
Every training-data pipeline MUST route candidate examples through
ContaminationGuard.from_evalsets_dir(Path("evalsets")) before writing
output, and MUST report the dropped count in its dataset manifest. A dataset
whose manifest lacks a decontamination entry does not get trained on.

chunks.title: Eval-Set Contamination Policy
chunks.heading: Direction of protection
chunks.text:
The guard protects eval questions from entering training inputs.
Corpus text itself is not contamination: eval questions were generated from
corpus chunks, and training pairs are generated from the same corpus — shared
source material is by design. What must never transfer is the question
(or a paraphrase of it), because that is what the eval measures generalization
against.

chunks.title: Eval-Set Contamination Policy
chunks.heading: Known limitations (accepted)
chunks.text:
- Semantic duplicates below 0.6 shingle Jaccard (aggressive rewording) can
  slip through. Embedding-similarity dedup was considered and deferred: the
  shingle check already catches same-generator paraphrases, and an embedding
  threshold adds a tunable free parameter with no labeled data to tune it on.
- The policy governs data this repo generates. It cannot say anything about
  the base model's (Qwen3-4B) pretraining corpus — base-model contamination
  is disclosed as a caveat in eval reports, not "solved".

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.text:
Generated 2026-11-02 by rype_evals.overturns from the committed
docs/reports/*-summary.json. Every number below is plucked from those files, so
this page cannot drift away from the reports it summarises. No network, no stack.

The short version. The stack here — hybrid RAG, a QLoRA fine-tune, a served
model, an eval harness — is not unusual. What is unusual is the record below:
eight claims this project believed, tested, and had to withdraw, each
published with the statistic that overturned it. Four of them were the project's
own prior conclusions; two were shipped defaults; one was the grader itself.

---

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 1. Sparse retrieval beats hybrid — the v2 ablation measured it.
chunks.text:
Wrong twice, in two different ways.

v2 raw set: sparse MRR@10 0.759 vs hybrid 0.705. v3 reworded queries: sparse falls to 0.611 (-0.149) while hybrid holds at 0.655 (-0.049) -- the 'win' was vocabulary leakage. Pooled graded labels: nDCG +0.008, p=0.573 -- a statistical tie.

What changed: Three chapters on one claim: a measured win, shown to be an artifact of the eval set, then shown to be no difference at all. Hybrid stayed the default for the robustness reason, not the original one.

Evidence: retrieval-ablation-v2 · retrieval-ablation-v3 · retrieval-golden-v1 · ADR-0019

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 2. Adding precision@k, recall@k and contextual precision makes the eval suite more rigorous.
chunks.text:
Three of them were the same column twice.

On single-gold-label sets recall@k == hit@k, precision@k == hit@k/k, and contextual precision == mrr@k. Verified per case across 3 datasets / 300 cases: the identities hold exactly, to the last bit of floating point (max deviation 0, against a 1e-12 tolerance). Three of the five new metrics carried no independent information, so they were not reported.

What changed: Implemented, tested, proven degenerate — and then not reported. The fix was better labels, not more metrics, which is what motivated the golden set.

Evidence: retrieval-metrics-audit-v1 · ADR-0018

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 3. hit@10 is a meaningful headline metric for this corpus.
chunks.text:
Saturated. It cannot separate anything.

All four retrieval modes score 0.97-0.99 on hit@10, and no pairwise difference is significant (worst p=1.000). The metric most prominent in the project's own earlier reports had no remaining power to separate anything.

What changed: Demoted from the headline. nDCG_graded@10 and recall@10 do the discriminating; hit@10 is reported only to show it is exhausted.

Evidence: retrieval-golden-v1 · ADR-0019

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 4. The shipped 350-token chunk size is the right default.
chunks.text:
It is not the best-measured option.

Re-parsing the real source documents under three chunk sizes: 150-token chunks beat the shipped 350-token default by nDCG +0.044 [+0.019, +0.074], p<0.001. Scope: 100/594 candidate documents (time-boxed, and said so).

What changed: A shipped default was contradicted by a measurement of the system's own corpus. Reported at document granularity, with the time-boxed scope stated.

Evidence: chunking-ablation-v1 · ADR-0020

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 5. The larger embedding model earns its cost.
chunks.text:
No measurable difference against one 3.1x smaller.

The incumbent (768-dim, 0.21 GB) is indistinguishable from a model 3.1x smaller (384-dim, 0.07 GB): nDCG -0.001 (p=0.943), recall -0.002 (p=0.929). The extra size was not earning its cost on this corpus.

What changed: Quality reported alongside indexing throughput, so 'no difference' becomes a cost decision rather than a shrug.

Evidence: embedding-ablation-v1 · ADR-0021

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 6. Concatenating conversation history will fix multi-turn retrieval.
chunks.text:
It does not. It trends worse.

Production retrieval ignores conversation history. The obvious fix -- concatenating the previous turn -- does not help: nDCG -0.074 (p=0.247), MRR -0.071 (p=0.301) across 50 two-turn conversations. It trends worse, not better. Published as a null result rather than assumed to work.

What changed: The intuitive fix was floor-tested before being shipped, and the null result was published with its significance test instead of being quietly dropped.

Evidence: multiturn-v1 · ADR-0020

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 7. The relevance judge is sound — it recovered 100% of seed chunks.
chunks.text:
It misses about half the relevant material. Seed recovery was the easy question.

Audited on a blinded, stratified sample. Against a second model rater (n=190) the judge looked systematically strict: signed error +0.327 [+0.226, +0.430], precision 0.968 against TPR 0.571. A human rater then labelled 40 of the same tasks and reproduced the direction and the capability number -- TPR 0.556 -- but not the magnitude: signed error +0.226 [-0.076, +0.571], which spans zero. Head to head the human grades 0.28 of a grade lower than the model (-0.279, excluding zero): the model rater was the lenient one, and its leniency inflated the offset.

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 7. The relevance judge is sound — it recovered 100% of seed chunks.
chunks.text:
What changed: Absolute recall/nDCG on the golden set read low, and the bias is near-equal across all four retrieval modes, so the published comparisons stand — the levels move, the deltas do not. Then the human labels overturned part of the overturn: the second-model rater had exaggerated the size of the offset, so the direction survives and the magnitude is back to being an open question.

Evidence: judge-validation-v1 · judge-validation-v2 · ADR-0022

chunks.title: Evidence index — how to read this repository
chunks.heading: The overturns › 8. A low recall@10 on the golden set means retrieval is failing.
chunks.text:
Most of what the metric flags is not a defect at all.

An over-inclusive signal flagged 28 of 100 queries as retrieval failures. Reading every one of them: 23 are not defects (82%) and only 5 are -- 5% of queries, not the 28% the flag rate implied. The largest category (18 cases) is queries where a grade-3 answer sits at rank 1-3 and recall@10 still scores them down because the corpus offers many acceptable answers per question. Coded by claude-opus-5, a language model, not a person.

What changed: The fix list changed completely. Nothing on it is motivated by raising recall@10, because most of what would raise that number would not help a user. What the aggregate had been hiding was its own composition: corpus redundancy and a metric penalising queries that were answered at rank 1.

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 1. System architecture
chunks.text:
The serving layer sits behind one OpenAI-compatible surface (/v1/chat/completions),
which is the single most important design decision: the gateway, the benchmark
harness, and the eval suite all speak it, so the engine underneath can change
without touching anything above it (ADR-0004, ADR-0011).

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 1. System architecture
chunks.text:
FastAPI gateway  (libs/core: cache · budget · fallback · tracing)
                 │  OpenAI-shaped messages in, SSE deltas out
                 ▼
        ┌──────────────── OpenAI-compatible /v1 surface ───────────────┐
        │                                                              │
  vLLM (Colab T4, ephemeral)                        Ollama / llama.cpp (Oracle ARM, always-on)
  PagedAttention · continuous batching              GGUF Q4 · single-stream · the public demo
  prefix cache · guided decoding · FP16/AWQ         no continuous batching
        │                                                              │
        └───────────────────────► OpsLM-v1 ◄───────────────────────────┘
                          Qwen3-4B QLoRA (r=16)

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 1. System architecture
chunks.text:
Two serving paths with different jobs (ADR-0016). A single path cannot be both
"always-on and free" and "demonstrates GPU inference engineering": the free
always-on host (Oracle Free Tier) is ARM CPU and can never run CUDA/vLLM. So
measurement runs on an ephemeral Colab T4 and is captured as a committed
artifact (raw JSON + report), while the always-on demo runs Ollama on CPU.
Every artifact states which hardware it describes — the demo's latency is the CPU
path; the report's latency is the T4 path, and conflating them would be the most
tempting dishonesty available here.

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 2. Inference flow (one request)
chunks.text:
A generation request is two regimes with very different cost, and the platform
measures them separately because they are moved by different optimizations:

1. Prefill — the prompt is processed in one forward pass; its output is
   TTFT (time to first token). Dominated by prompt length and by whether the
   prompt's prefix is already in the KV cache. *Measured: vLLM FP16 TTFT p50
   59 ms at concurrency 1.*
2. Decode — tokens are produced one at a time, each attending to the growing
   KV cache; the per-token gap is ITL / TPOT (inter-token latency). This is
   what continuous batching and speculative decoding move; TTFT is not. *Measured:
   vLLM FP16 ITL p50 ≈ 50–60 ms.*

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 2. Inference flow (one request)
chunks.text:
Tokens stream back over SSE as they decode. The harness measures TTFT from the
first streamed chunk and reconstructs ITL as (latency − TTFT) / (tokens − 1),
so the two regimes never get averaged into one misleading "latency" figure.

KV cache & PagedAttention. The dominant memory cost during decode is the KV
cache (per-token key/value tensors for every layer). vLLM's PagedAttention stores
it in fixed-size pages instead of one contiguous buffer, which is what makes the
next two features possible — pages can be shared (prefix caching) and packed
across requests (continuous batching) without contiguous-allocation waste.

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 2. Inference flow (one request)
chunks.text:
Prefix caching. Requests that share a long prefix (a fixed system prompt, or a
retrieved document reused across turns — exactly the RAG workload) reuse the
prefix's KV pages, so the second+ request skips prefilling it. *Measured, with a
control: vLLM 47.8% TTFT reduction with the cache on vs 0.0% with
--no-enable-prefix-caching — the control run is what proves the number is the
cache and not warm-up.*

Guided decoding. For structured output, the engine masks the token logits to
only those the JSON schema permits, so the result parses by construction. *Measured:
vLLM JSON parse rate 0 → 1.00 (off → on); Ollama's OpenAI endpoint does not
honor response_format, so it cannot be constrained (0 → 0.0).*

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 3. Scaling strategy
chunks.text:
Continuous batching is the scaling story on a single device. Instead of
running requests one at a time, the engine interleaves many requests' decode steps
into shared forward passes, admitting and retiring them token-by-token. The payoff
is measured directly by sweeping concurrency 1 → 16:

| Config | Throughput scaling (1→16) | p95 latency inflation | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| vLLM FP16 | 13.4× | 0.81× | concurrent requests share decode passes — throughput scales while tail latency holds |
| Ollama Q4 | 0.89× | 16.0× | no continuous batching — requests serialize, throughput flat, latency grows linearly |

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 3. Scaling strategy
chunks.text:
Same model, same T4, same harness: the delta is the engine. This is the clearest
evidence in the project of why a dedicated serving engine matters. (Note the
honest nuance: Ollama is faster single-stream — 3.6 s vs 13.0 s at concurrency
1, because Q4 is lighter than FP16 — but collapses under load. The engine choice is
a load-shape decision, not a blanket "faster/slower".)

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 3. Scaling strategy
chunks.text:
Beyond one T4 [design]. A single free T4 cannot demonstrate the next tiers, so
they are described, not claimed:
- Tensor parallelism — shard a model too large for one GPU across devices
  (--tensor-parallel-size); needs ≥2 GPUs.
- Horizontal replicas — stateless vLLM replicas behind a load balancer; the
  gateway already speaks the OpenAI surface, so this is a deployment change, not a
  code change (infra/k8s has the manifests).
- KV-cache pressure — the real ceiling on concurrency is KV memory, not FLOPs;
  --gpu-memory-utilization and --max-model-len are the levers, and quantized
  KV / paged offload are the next steps.

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 4. Failure handling
chunks.text:
The serving path is designed to fail legibly, consistent with the RAG stack's
degradation ladder:

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 4. Failure handling
chunks.text:
- Server not ready. The benchmark/serve harness blocks on /v1/models and
  runs a single smoke request before load-testing, so "up but not generating"
  (e.g. a bad launch flag) fails in seconds with the real HTTP error rather than
  as 32 silent timeouts.
- Generation failure. The gateway tries models in order, but only until the
  first token reaches the client — a mid-stream provider failure surfaces as an
  error rather than silently splicing two answers together (libs/core/llm.py).
- Cold start / OOM. vLLM reserves KV memory at launch (--gpu-memory-utilization
  0.85); if another process holds VRAM the engine fails fast at startup rather
  than thrashing. (Observed live: a still-running vLLM starved a co-located Ollama
  to 80% CPU — the fix is to free the GPU before switching engines, now enforced.)

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 4. Failure handling
chunks.text:
- Quality floor under quantization. Speed is never accepted without its quality
  cost: each quant is meant to re-run the Phase-4 eval, and the Pareto frontier
  excludes any config without a quality score so "faster" can't silently mean
  "worse" (benchmarks/report.py).

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 5. Tradeoffs
chunks.text:
| Decision | Chosen | Cost accepted | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Serving engine | vLLM for measurement, Ollama for the always-on demo | two paths to keep honest about | free-tier ARM can't run CUDA; the split is the only way to have both always-on-free and real GPU numbers (ADR-0016) |
| Quantization | FP16 benchmarked; GGUF Q4 serves the demo | Q4 trades some quality for ~4× smaller + faster single-stream | Q4 fits the CPU demo host and wins single-stream; FP16 is the fidelity reference. The frontier (pending a quality axis) picks the knee, not the fastest |
| AWQ | dropped | one fewer quant on the frontier | AutoAWQ is unmaintained past torch 2.6 and threw cascading conflicts on Colab's torch 2.11; recorded honestly rather than forced |

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 5. Tradeoffs
chunks.text:
| Decision | Chosen | Cost accepted | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Abstraction | one OpenAI-compatible surface | a thin indirection layer | swapping engines/quants becomes config, not a rewrite; one harness measures them all |
| Measurement | committed JSON + generated report | must re-run to refresh | a latency number without committed provenance (hardware, n, date) is a rumour, not a result |

chunks.title: Inference System — Technical Design
chunks.heading: 6. What is measured vs. designed
chunks.text:
| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Continuous batching 13.4× / prefix cache 47.8% / guided 0→1.0 | measured (T4, committed JSON) |
| Cross-engine contrast (vLLM vs Ollama) | measured (same T4, same harness) |
| Before/after eval (base vs OpsLM), quant→quality frontier | pending — needs a served-model eval pass |
| Tensor parallelism, multi-replica scaling | [design] — a single T4 can't show it; stated, not faked |

chunks.title: Chat Latency Budget & Degradation Ladder
chunks.text:
Applies to POST /v1/chat (SSE). Budgets are targets on the dev stack
(CPU-only embeddings/reranker, Gemini free tier); measured numbers live in the
request_ledger table (latency_ms, first_token_ms) and, later, Langfuse
(Phase 8).

chunks.title: Chat Latency Budget & Degradation Ladder
chunks.heading: Budget vs. measured (2026-07-12, dev stack, warm process)
chunks.text:
| Stage | Target | Measured | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retrieval total: embed + hybrid search, no rerank (default since ablation v1) | ≤ 300 ms warm | ~60 ms | chat_retrieval_timeout_s (10 s hard cap) |
| Retrieval with rerank (opt-in, RYPE_CHAT_RERANK) | — | ~2.7 s @ k=6, ~9 s @ k=10 (CPU cross-encoder; measured quality-negative — see retrieval-ablation-v1) | same |
| LLM first token (Gemini 3.5-flash free tier) | provider-bound | 7–19 s, grows with prompt size | chat_llm_timeout_s |
| First streamed token, end to end | < 2 s (paid/local serving) | ~18–23 s on free tier | measured (first_token_ms in ledger) |
| Full answer | ≤ 45 s hard cap | ~19–24 s | chat_llm_timeout_s |

chunks.title: Chat Latency Budget & Degradation Ladder
chunks.heading: Budget vs. measured (2026-07-12, dev stack, warm process)
chunks.text:
Honest reading: the < 2 s first-token target is not achievable on the free
tier — the provider queue alone exceeds it — so it is stated as the target
for paid or local (OpsLM/Ollama, Phase 5–7) serving, and the free-tier numbers
are recorded as measured baselines in request_ledger. Our own stack's share
is the ~2.7 s warm retrieval (CPU rerank ~2.5 s of it; GPU or a smaller
reranker are the Phase 7 levers), plus a one-off ~10 s cold start to load
embedding + reranker models on the first request after boot.

chunks.title: Chat Latency Budget & Degradation Ladder
chunks.heading: Degradation ladder
chunks.text:
Failures degrade quality; they do not 500. Each step down is recorded in the
degraded list on the sources and done SSE events, and in
request_ledger.status / meta.degraded.

| Step | Condition | Behaviour | degraded marker |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | happy path | hybrid retrieval + rerank → grounded, cited answer | — |
| 2 | rerank fails or retrieval times out | retry hybrid retrieval without rerank | rerank_skipped |
| 3 | retrieval fails entirely (Qdrant down, embedder broken) | deterministic abstention, no model call, no citations, done status abstained | retrieval_skipped |
| 4 | LLM fails (all models in the fallback chain, or mid-stream) | error SSE event; ledger row with status=error | — |

chunks.title: Chat Latency Budget & Degradation Ladder
chunks.heading: Degradation ladder
chunks.text:
Provider fallback (chat_fallback_models, e.g. Groq) happens inside step 4's
"all models" clause: the next model is tried only if the current one produced
no tokens yet — once tokens have streamed, switching providers would splice
two answers, so we fail instead (see ADR-0004).

An empty successful retrieval also abstains before generation. These SSE semantics
are separate from the browser workspace and its optional structured JSON endpoint.

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.text:
The README leads with what the project does. This page holds every boundary on those
claims, in one place, so none of them is lost. The full falsification record (claims the
project tested and withdrew) is in evidence.md; the per-claim status table
is in claims.md.

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.heading: Security scope
chunks.text:
See the Status / open column of the threat model. In short:
the regex injection layer cannot catch rewording, translation or encodings, and with the
optional LLM classifier added the layered detector still catches only 45% [33%, 58%] of a public
benchmark's attacks (docs/reports/security-classifier-v1.md); credential redaction is
pattern-based; embedding model files are hash-pinned, but only for the pinned revisions; the
Kubernetes manifests pass Trivy but have not been applied to a live cluster; rate limits
stop single-source abuse, not distributed abuse; the deployment is single-tenant.

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.heading: Security scope
chunks.text:
The agent eval (docs/reports/agent-v1.md) uses 16 synthetic single-fault scenarios and one
model; harness v2 was changed after seeing the first ten, so only the six held-out scenarios
measure generalization, and their interval is wide (6/6, [0.61, 1.00]). Planted log text can
still derail a diagnosis (5/80), and evidence quotes are checked for existence, not support.

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.heading: Public workspace
chunks.text:
The default analysis runs in the browser over six official documents / 180 passages.
It does not upload diagnostic text or execute commands; normal hosting access logs
still apply. Credential-pattern redaction is best-effort: sanitize input first. The
optional model path validates JSON, source IDs, exact quotes, output completion and
permitted read-only command forms. Those checks do not prove factual support. No model
endpoint is configured on the public deployment. /model-demo is a separately labelled
sample console and is not part of the evidence workflow.

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.heading: Serving-evidence corrections (October 2026)
chunks.text:
The repository already contained hybrid retrieval, ingestion, model training and
inference experiments. This redevelopment makes one small workflow usable and
corrects the decision logic behind serving claims:

- Capacity admission checks errors, successful sample counts, finite latency and
  throughput, and count consistency. Defaults: zero errors and at least 20 successes.
  Twenty observations are a bounded minimum, not precise p95 uncertainty estimation.
- Repeatability requires complete matching identities and distinct run IDs.
  Cache settings and request counts cannot be pooled. Historical identities are
  incomplete, so historical repeatability is not measured.
- CI rebuilds the browser corpus through the actual ingestion pipeline and reruns
  the same retrieval function used by the browser, starting from raw documents.

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.heading: Reproducible evidence
chunks.text:
| Result | Scope and limitations |
|---|---|
| Term overlap: 15/16 document hit@1, 16/16 hit@3 | Synthetic agent-authored questions, specified before the first run; six docs / 180 passages. Document labels do not establish passage answer quality. Selection used these results; cases are now public regression data. |
| BM25: 14/16 hit@1, 16/16 hit@3 | Same inputs. No significant superiority claim. The simpler term-overlap ranker ships. |
| 4/4 negative cases empty | One empty and three unrelated queries; not calibrated answerability or security evidence. |
| Historical vLLM FP16: 233.18 reported tokens/s at c=16; Ollama Q4: 37.22 at c=1 | Recomputed stored T4 summaries under p95 TTFT ≤1s, latency ≤30s, zero errors, ≥20 successes. Not new GPU measurements; engine and precision both differ. |

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.heading: Reproducible evidence
chunks.text:
Per-case retrieval report ·
Capacity decisions and reasons.
Stress queries demonstrate vocabulary mismatch and tangential matches. Instruction-like
queries can match ordinary text. The app presents excerpts, not diagnoses or safety verdicts.

chunks.title: Limitations and scope
chunks.heading: Research boundaries
chunks.text:
- Retrieval studies are stored experiments, not newly
  rerun model studies. Preserve original dataset scope and judge limitations.
- OpsLM-v1 is a published SFT artifact
  (534 train / 59 validation pairs). A matched base-versus-SFT task-quality gain is

- Historical serving dashboard: 13.4× is
  within-vLLM c=1→16 scaling. Cross-engine comparisons do not isolate scheduling;

- Model demo shows labeled samples without an

chunks.title: Model registry — RYPE
chunks.text:
Generated by registry/registry.py from registry/models.json, with
latency/throughput joined from benchmarks/results/ and eval scores from

chunks.title: Runbook navigator architecture
chunks.text:
The user is an engineer finding an official passage while learning or troubleshooting
Kubernetes. No external users or partner corpus are assumed.

The manifest pins upstream revision and SHA-256 for six raw Markdown files.
rype_evals.runbook_fixture verifies each hash and calls ingest_bytes: parsing,
section-aware chunking, quality/deduplication, secret redaction, injection quarantine.
It fails if a document yields no usable chunks. Each passage retains document ID,
section, pinned source and canonical URL. CI compares the generated JSON byte-for-byte.

chunks.title: Runbook navigator architecture
chunks.text:
Next.js serves that static corpus. Browser and evaluator import the same module.
Default ranking counts distinct query-term overlap with deterministic ID tie-breaking;
two matching terms are required when a query has at least two. BM25 is an evaluated
alternative (k1=1.2, b=0.75). Neither score is a confidence or answerability probability.

React displays escaped original text; Markdown and HTML are not executed. Excerpts
may retain upstream template markers or refer to unbundled code examples. Follow the
source link for context. Query edits clear old results; result focus moves into view.
Loading/retry, empty, malformed and oversized-input states are explicit.

chunks.title: Runbook navigator architecture
chunks.text:
No model, vector server, database or search API runs for a browser query. Questions are
not uploaded by the search code, although hosting access logs apply to asset requests.
No cluster commands execute. The separate model sample console validates input, bounds
conversation size, times out calls and reports upstream failures; its proxy does not retrieve.

chunks.title: Runbook navigator architecture
chunks.heading: Evaluation and limits
chunks.text:
Six development, 16 initially held-out positive, four negative (one empty), and four
stress queries were specified before the first metric run. The agent authored synthetic
questions and coarse document labels; this is not independent human assessment.
Selection between rankers used those results. Future improvements need new independent
passage labels and a fresh holdout for generalization claims.

Hit@k does not establish answer correctness. Generic words can return tangential passages;
paraphrases can miss. Limited coverage cannot answer arbitrary Kubernetes questions.
Pinned docs age while current links change. Stress cases remain in the report. No generated
answer quality, model-training gain or attack resistance is established by these tests.

chunks.title: Runbook navigator architecture
chunks.heading: Evaluation and limits
chunks.text:
CI exercises raw-input parity, actual ranker tests, both baselines and the production build.
A deliberate empty chunker fails fixture generation; removing passage text changes retrieval.
These checks complement the existing Qdrant smoke test rather than replacing the full stack.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.text:
The public homepage is an evidence workflow: sanitized symptom and optional diagnostic
text -> recognized status signatures -> up to three pinned official passages ->
exportable JSON brief. /runbooks exposes general passage search; /engineering
explains decisions; /study exposes recorded evidence and limitations.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Implementation contract
chunks.text:
opslm-demo/lib/troubleshoot.mjs supplies preparation, best-effort credential-pattern
redaction, signal recognition, bounded retrieval context, prompt construction and
output validation. The browser uses it directly without transmitting diagnostic
text. Six raw official documents flow through the existing Python ingestion pipeline
into 180 passages. The generated corpus is checked against raw inputs in CI.

The export contains the redacted issue, up to 2,000 diagnostic characters, detected
signals, retrieved passages, source links, and analysis mode. Input limits are 500
issue characters and 12,000 diagnostic characters. Signal recognition scans the
allowed input; context truncation is displayed. Redaction is incomplete: users must
sanitize secrets before pasting. Normal hosting request logs still apply.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Optional generation (not enabled on the public deployment)
chunks.text:
No models were loaded for this release, at the project owner's request. The public
workflow needs no model or paid service. To connect an already running local
OpenAI-compatible server when resources permit, configure these server-only variables:

text
RYPE_TROUBLESHOOT_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8011/v1
RYPE_TROUBLESHOOT_MODEL=your-local-model-name
# RYPE_TROUBLESHOOT_API_KEY is optional for an authenticated endpoint


Then run the Next.js application locally. Endpoint configuration does not verify
availability. The explicit model button sends locally redacted input to this app's
server, which redacts again before calling the configured endpoint. It never inherits
the separate sample console's endpoint. Production localhost cannot reach a user's
computer. No hosted inference or infrastructure is provisioned by these instructions.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Optional generation (not enabled on the public deployment)
chunks.text:
/api/troubleshoot invokes the shared troubleshoot-http.mjs handler. It rejects
malformed or oversized input; bounds context to three passages / 6,000 characters;
uses temperature 0, seed 42, max_tokens 384, and a 55-second upstream timeout.
With no supporting passages it abstains before calling a model. With no endpoint
it returns excerpts. Upstream, schema or completion failures return 502 without a
fabricated answer. Successful output requires recognized status, bounded arrays,
real source IDs and matching 20-600 character quotes. Command suggestions pass a
restricted kubectl get/describe/logs/rollout status/history grammar. No commands run.
These structural checks establish provenance, not factual entailment, command
relevance, or a security certification. A model can still misinterpret real quotes.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Optional generation (not enabled on the public deployment)
chunks.text:
The separate Python SSE RAG service also abstains when retrieval fails or returns
no chunks; tests assert no model call in those paths.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Evaluation and reproduction
chunks.text:
bash
uv run python -m rype_evals.troubleshooting_contamination --check
node opslm-demo/scripts/build-study.mjs --check
node opslm-demo/scripts/model-study.mjs --label excerpts --out /tmp/excerpts.json
cd opslm-demo && npm test && npm run build

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Evaluation and reproduction
chunks.text:
The runner calls the same HTTP handler as the application and records every case,
errors, source IDs, prompt/implementation/data hashes, commit and dirty state.
The 30 synthetic scenarios (6 development / 24 held-out) were frozen in commit
19f2295 before model inference. The lexical contamination report checks all 30
against the actual 593 committed SFT inputs: no exact or thresholded 5-gram overlap
was flagged. Semantic and pretraining overlap are unknown. Reference phrase coverage
in returned passages is not generated-answer accuracy; excerpt mode cannot answer
questions or satisfy answer-status labels. No base/SFT improvement is reported.
The independent pinned GGUF conversions would confound a causal training claim.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Recorded excerpt-only run
chunks.text:
Per-case report: clean commit
2f88668fb9b0eeb469ff6d70e6b2c47899aa0839 completed all 24 held-out requests with HTTP 200 and
zero generated answers. Returned passages covered 31 of 32 reference phrase groups;
this measures lexical presence, not whether an answer is correct. Three cases
abstained with no passages. A Redis out-of-scope scenario still retrieved tangential
Kubernetes material: nonempty retrieval must not be read as answerability. No cases
were removed or tuned after this run.

chunks.title: Incident investigation workspace
chunks.heading: Recorded excerpt-only run
chunks.text:
The memory onboarding example asks specifically how Kubernetes enforces container
memory limits. During production mobile QA, its earlier vague question ranked a
deployment-rollout passage first. The more specific example ranks the resource-limit
enforcement section first. This is an onboarding correction, not a retrieval algorithm
change or a held-out quality gain; vague user questions can still match tangential text.

internet

chunks.title: ADR-0001: Monorepo with uv workspaces
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
RYPE spans an API service, a web UI, an MCP server, training scripts, and several shared
Python libraries (ingestion, RAG, evals, security). These pieces share Pydantic schemas and
settings, and they evolve together — a chunking change touches ingestion, RAG, and evals in
one commit.

chunks.title: ADR-0001: Monorepo with uv workspaces
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
One repository, managed as a uv workspace: apps under apps/, shared libraries under
libs/, each with its own pyproject.toml, one shared lockfile at the root.

chunks.title: ADR-0001: Monorepo with uv workspaces
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- Cross-cutting changes (schema + consumers) land atomically; no version dance between repos.
- uv sync gives every developer and CI job an identical environment from one uv.lock.
- Workspace source dependencies (rype-core = { workspace = true }) keep imports honest —
  apps consume libraries through declared dependencies, not path hacks.
- Tradeoff: CI runs the whole workspace on every PR. Acceptable at this scale; if it slows,
  add path-filtered jobs rather than splitting repos.

chunks.title: ADR-0001: Monorepo with uv workspaces
chunks.heading: Alternatives considered
chunks.text:
- Polyrepo — rejected: version-pinning overhead across 5+ internal packages for a
  single-developer project buys isolation nobody needs.
- Poetry/pip-tools monorepo — rejected: no first-class workspace concept; uv's is native,
  and uv is also the fastest installer for CI.

chunks.title: ADR-0002: Qdrant over pgvector and Pinecone
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Phase 3 requires hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse/BM25-style), rich metadata filtering
(tool, version, doc type), and local-first operation under Docker Compose with zero hosting
budget.

chunks.title: ADR-0002: Qdrant over pgvector and Pinecone
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Qdrant, one collection with named dense + sparse vectors (BGE-M3 produces both), payload
metadata for filtering.

chunks.title: ADR-0002: Qdrant over pgvector and Pinecone
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- Hybrid search is a single engine feature (server-side fusion of named vectors), not a
  client-side merge of two systems — simpler ranking code and one operational dependency.
- Filtered search is first-class and indexed; version-awareness filters (Phase 11) come free.
- Runs in Compose with a volume; the same image deploys anywhere later.
- Tradeoff: one more service to operate versus pgvector-inside-Postgres. Accepted because
  pgvector has no native sparse-vector/hybrid story, which would force a bolt-on BM25 layer.

chunks.title: ADR-0002: Qdrant over pgvector and Pinecone
chunks.heading: Alternatives considered
chunks.text:
- pgvector — rejected for missing native sparse/hybrid support; would need pg_search or
  app-side RRF over tsvector, spreading retrieval logic across two query languages.
- Pinecone — rejected: hosted-only conflicts with the free-tier constraint and the
  local-first demo story; also weaker as a portfolio signal than operating the store yourself.
- Revisit if corpus scale or ops burden changes; the retrieval interface in libs/rag keeps
  the store swappable.

chunks.title: ADR-0003: fastembed + bge-base-en-v1.5 dense / BM25 sparse for hybrid retrieval
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Retrieval needs dense + sparse vectors, produced locally at zero cost, on CPU,
on a Windows/WSL dev machine. The original plan named BGE-M3 (which emits both
dense and sparse vectors) via fastembed.

chunks.title: ADR-0003: fastembed + bge-base-en-v1.5 dense / BM25 sparse for hybrid retrieval
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
- Runtime: fastembed (ONNX) — no PyTorch dependency (~2GB saved), fast CPU
  inference, one library for dense + sparse + reranking.
- Dense: BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 (768d) — fastembed 0.8 does not ship
  BGE-M3 for dense embedding (verified via TextEmbedding.list_supported_models()),
  so the plan's model was unavailable in the chosen runtime. bge-base beats
  bge-large on CPU latency ~3× with a small quality gap, and the corpus is
  English-only technical documentation.
- Sparse: Qdrant/bm25 — term-frequency vectors with IDF applied
  server-side by Qdrant (Modifier.IDF); classic BM25 keyword behaviour.
- Reranker: BAAI/bge-reranker-base (bge-reranker-v2-m3 likewise not in
  fastembed's supported list).
- Fusion: RRF server-side in Qdrant over the two named vectors.

chunks.title: ADR-0003: fastembed + bge-base-en-v1.5 dense / BM25 sparse for hybrid retrieval
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
All four choices are RYPE_* settings, not code constants; swapping to a
sentence-transformers/BGE-M3 stack later is an embedder implementation +
re-embed sweep, nothing else.

chunks.title: ADR-0003: fastembed + bge-base-en-v1.5 dense / BM25 sparse for hybrid retrieval
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- Whole retrieval stack runs pip-install-light and CPU-only; embedding ~400
  chunks takes minutes, not hours.
- 768d dense vectors (vs 1024d planned): smaller index, slightly lower ceiling;
  retrieval evaluation in Phase 3 will quantify whether an upgrade is worth it.
- Multilingual queries lose dense quality (bge-base is English); accepted for
  this corpus.

chunks.title: ADR-0004: Chat serving — thin LiteLLM SDK client, SSE events, pre-first-token fallback
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Phase 3 needs /v1/chat: retrieval-grounded, citation-bearing answers streamed
to clients, on free-tier LLM APIs (Gemini primary; Groq later as fallback). The
approved plan defers the full LiteLLM proxy (routing, budgets, caching) to
Phase 6. Decisions needed now: how to call providers, the wire protocol for
streaming, and what happens when a provider fails.

chunks.title: ADR-0004: Chat serving — thin LiteLLM SDK client, SSE events, pre-first-token fallback
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
1. LiteLLM SDK directly (litellm.acompletion), not the proxy.
   rype_core.llm.LiteLLMClient is a ~150-line wrapper that is already
   OpenAI-shaped, so the Phase 6 proxy swap is a config change (point at the
   proxy's base URL) rather than a rewrite. Running the proxy now would add a
   service to the compose stack with none of its value used yet.
   API keys are passed explicitly from Settings (pydantic-settings reads
   .env without exporting to os.environ, so relying on litellm's implicit
   env lookup would silently break under uvicorn).

chunks.title: ADR-0004: Chat serving — thin LiteLLM SDK client, SSE events, pre-first-token fallback
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
2. SSE with typed events, not a bare token stream. POST /v1/chat emits
   sources (all retrieved chunks, numbered — sent before generation so the
   UI can render citations as [n] markers arrive), then delta events, then
   exactly one done (model, cited indices, tokens, cost, latency) or error.
   SSE over WebSocket for the base path: it works through proxies/curl, and
   the client→server direction isn't needed until image upload (which gets a
   WebSocket variant later, per plan).

3. Provider fallback only before the first token. The fallback chain
   (chat_model + chat_fallback_models) advances only while nothing has
   been streamed. After first delta, a provider failure surfaces as an error
   event: silently switching mid-answer would splice two models' outputs and
   corrupt citations.

chunks.title: ADR-0004: Chat serving — thin LiteLLM SDK client, SSE events, pre-first-token fallback
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
4. Degradation over failure for retrieval (skip rerank → skip retrieval →
   error), with every step recorded on the events and in request_ledger —
   see docs/latency-budget.md.

5. request_ledger starts now (migration 0002), not in Phase 6: tokens,
   cost (litellm price table; free-tier rows still record what it would
   cost), latency, first-token latency, degradation markers. Phase 4's
   production metrics and Phase 6's cost panel read from it; starting it with
   the first LLM-touching endpoint means the cost story has data from day one.

chunks.title: ADR-0004: Chat serving — thin LiteLLM SDK client, SSE events, pre-first-token fallback
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
6. Model: gemini/gemini-3.5-flash, reasoning_effort=minimal. The
   planned gemini-2.5-flash now 404s for new API keys ("no longer available
   to new users"), and gemini-2.0-flash has free-tier quota 0. 3.5-flash
   thinks by default (measured: 89 reasoning tokens for a one-word reply);
   minimal drops that to zero, which is the right default for grounded RAG
   synthesis where latency matters more than multi-step reasoning. Both are
   settings (chat_model, chat_reasoning_effort), and we pin a concrete
   model rather than the floating gemini-flash-latest alias so eval numbers
   stay attributable to a model version.
   Quota reality (measured 2026-07-12): the free tier caps 3.5-flash at
   20 requests/day (GenerateRequestsPerDayPerProjectPerModel-FreeTier).
   Consequences: chat_fallback_models defaults to gemini-3.1-flash-lite

chunks.title: ADR-0004: Chat serving — thin LiteLLM SDK client, SSE events, pre-first-token fallback
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
(separate, much larger quota) so interactive chat degrades from "best
   model" to "lite model" instead of erroring; bulk offline jobs (eval-set
   generation, judging) default to the lite model via eval_generator_model
   and must never point at the 20/day quality model.

chunks.title: ADR-0004: Chat serving — thin LiteLLM SDK client, SSE events, pre-first-token fallback
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- Phase 6 keeps LiteLLMClient's interface and re-points it at the proxy;
  routing/caching/budget logic stays out of the API service.
- Non-streaming mode (stream: false) returns the same pipeline as one JSON
  document — the eval harnesses (retrieval eval, RAGAS) consume this instead
  of parsing SSE.
- Known limitation: gemini free tier is ~10–15 RPM; there is no rate limiting
  or caching until Phase 6, so bulk eval runs must batch and back off
  themselves (the Phase 4 harness does).

chunks.title: ADR-0005: CI eval gate = pinned thresholds + committed retrieval fixture
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Phase 4 requires a CI gate that fails PRs which regress RAG quality. The full
eval stack cannot run in GitHub Actions as-is: the corpus lives in a DVC
remote on local MinIO (unreachable from Actions), and the LLM-judged
metrics need Gemini free-tier quota that is shared with development —
gemini-3.5-flash allows 20 requests/day total, and even flash-lite's
larger quota is the same pool the dataset-generation pipelines draw from.

Options considered for getting eval data into CI:

chunks.title: ADR-0005: CI eval gate = pinned thresholds + committed retrieval fixture
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
- (a) Google Drive DVC remote — reachable from Actions, but adds OAuth
  secret management and an external dependency for a 7 MB dataset, and every
  CI run would pull the full corpus to test a fraction of it.
- (b) Committed trimmed fixture — a 200-chunk subset (25 gold chunks for
  the first 25 frozen retrieval-v1 cases + 175 seeded distractors) committed
  to git (~300 KB). Embedding it with CPU fastembed takes ~50 s.
- (c) Nightly-only gate on a self-hosted runner — full fidelity, but
  loses the per-PR gate entirely and adds runner maintenance; the machine in
  question is a personal laptop that is often off.

chunks.title: ADR-0005: CI eval gate = pinned thresholds + committed retrieval fixture
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Option (b), structured as two deterministic, secret-free layers in
eval-gate.yml:

1. rype_evals.regression — asserts every committed
   docs/reports/*-summary.json against pinned thresholds
   (evalsets/regression-thresholds.json). Thresholds are pinned to measured
   baselines minus explicit slack; a missing report/mode/metric is a failure,
   not a skip. This stops "the numbers quietly changed/disappeared" PRs.
2. rype_evals.ci_retrieval_smoke — embeds the committed fixture
   into a Qdrant service container and runs the 25 frozen cases in hybrid
   mode, asserting live: true thresholds. This catches real retrieval-stack
   regressions (chunking, fusion, store queries, embedder config) on every
   PR, not just report edits.

chunks.title: ADR-0005: CI eval gate = pinned thresholds + committed retrieval fixture
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
LLM-judged quality (faithfulness/relevance via rag_suite) stays a
local/manual gate for now, recorded in Postgres eval_runs and committed
as report artifacts that layer 1 then protects. This is a deliberate
free-tier tradeoff, not an oversight: a per-PR judge run would either starve
development of quota or silently skip on forks without secrets — a gate that
sometimes doesn't run is worse than a documented manual step.

chunks.title: ADR-0005: CI eval gate = pinned thresholds + committed retrieval fixture
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- PRs touching retrieval/eval/API code get a real quality gate in ~3–4 min
  (fastembed model download is cached on uv.lock).
- The fixture is intentionally easy (200 chunks → MRR ≈ 0.85 vs 0.64 on the
  full corpus): its job is regression detection, not benchmarking. Absolute
  numbers live in the ablation reports.
- Fixture regeneration (build_ci_fixture, seeded) is only needed when the
  frozen evalset or corpus export format changes; regenerating re-pins the
  retrieval-ci-smoke thresholds against fresh measurements.
- When a hosted DVC remote or paid API budget arrives, layer 2 can grow into
  the full suite without changing the gate's shape (thresholds file + exit
  code stay the interface).

chunks.title: ADR-0006: Prompt-variant testing via the existing eval stack, not promptfoo
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
The Phase 4 plan listed "promptfoo for prompt-variant testing" alongside the
RAGAS-style judged suite and the regression gate. Those two now exist and run
(rag_suite → eval_runs + pinned thresholds; eval-gate.yml green on Actions).
The question left: adopt promptfoo for comparing chat-prompt variants, or
close the gap another way.

What prompt-variant testing must deliver here:
1. Regression protection — a prompt edit that hurts answer quality must
   fail a gate before it ships.
2. Side-by-side comparison — when someone proposes a prompt change,
   variant A vs variant B numbers on the same cases.

chunks.title: ADR-0006: Prompt-variant testing via the existing eval stack, not promptfoo
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Do not adopt promptfoo. Cover the two needs with what exists:

1. Regression protection is already live: the chat prompt cannot change
   without the judged smoke (rag_suite) being re-run — its report is pinned
   in evalsets/regression-thresholds.json (faithfulness ≥ 0.9, relevance
   ≥ 0.85, citation_used ≥ 0.9), and the regression gate fails on any
   committed report below threshold. The workflow for a prompt PR is:
   re-run the smoke, commit the regenerated report, gate must stay green.
2. Side-by-side comparison, when actually needed, is two rag_suite runs —
   one per prompt variant — compared as eval_runs rows (same dataset, same
   judge, run params recorded). The Postgres judge cache makes the unchanged
   halves of repeated runs free. No new tooling is required to read two rows.

chunks.title: ADR-0006: Prompt-variant testing via the existing eval stack, not promptfoo
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Why promptfoo specifically lost:
- Judge quota: promptfoo's LLM-graded assertions bypass our Postgres
  judge cache, and free-tier quota is the platform's scarcest resource —
  a second, uncached judging path is a real cost, not a convenience.
- Duplicate config surface: it would re-declare providers/models outside
  libs/core settings (fallback chains, reasoning-effort quirks, the
  litellm <1.92 pin), which is exactly the drift the thin LiteLLM client
  (ADR-0004) exists to prevent.
- Node dependency in the Python eval path for a capability we exercise
  rarely (the chat prompt has changed twice in the project's life).

chunks.title: ADR-0006: Prompt-variant testing via the existing eval stack, not promptfoo
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- Prompt iteration stays quota-cheap and lands in the same eval_runs/reports
  surface the UI and gate already read.
- We give up promptfoo's matrix ergonomics (many variants × many asserts in
  one YAML). If prompt work ever becomes high-frequency (e.g. Phase 5 OpsLM
  prompt tuning), the revisit trigger is: >2 variants compared per week —
  then a thin --system-prompt override on rag_suite is the first step,
  promptfoo the second.
- The plan's Phase 4 checklist item is closed by this ADR rather than by a
  dependency.

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Phase 9 requires defenses against the attacks a RAG platform actually faces:
1. Indirect prompt injection — instructions planted in ingested documents
   (the serious one: retrieval hands attacker text straight to the LLM).
2. Credential leakage — secrets in ingested docs get embedded, retrieved,
   and quoted into answers.
3. Direct query injection — override/exfiltration attempts typed into chat.

The plan named Presidio (PII) and Rebuff-style detection as candidates.

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Three layers in libs/security, all deterministic, all measured or unit-tested:

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
1. Ingest quarantine (primary defense). Every document is scanned by a
   weighted-signal injection heuristic (scan_injection); a flagged document
   is stored with status=quarantined and contributes zero chunks to
   retrieval. Poisoned docs are stopped before they can ever reach a prompt.
2. Ingest-time secret redaction. Credential-shaped strings (AWS key ids,
   GitHub/Slack/Google/OpenAI tokens, private-key blocks, JWTs, long assigned
   api_key=/secret_key= values) are replaced with [REDACTED:]
   before storage/embedding, so nothing downstream — Qdrant payloads, chat
   context, exports — ever holds them. Counted per ingest job
   (secrets_redacted in stats).
3. Query-time flagging, not blocking. Chat queries are scanned and the
   tripped signal names land in request_ledger.meta.injection_flags for

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
audit/alerting. We deliberately do NOT block: this is read-only RAG (no
   tools mutate anything), and DevOps vocabulary ("override the entrypoint",
   "ignore files", "system:masters", "forget cached layers") makes heuristic
   blocking an FPR trap that would break legitimate use.

The heuristic is treated as a classifier with an eval. A frozen red-team
set (evalsets/security-redteam-v1.jsonl: 15 attacks, 18 benign DevOps
sentences chosen to share surface vocabulary with attacks) is scored by
python -m rype_security.evaluate; measured 2026-07-17: TPR 1.0,
specificity 1.0, precision 1.0. Thresholds pinned in the regression gate
(TPR ≥ 0.85, specificity ≥ 0.95). The set is small and hand-curated — the
claim is "commodity attacks are caught and measured", not "injection solved".

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: What we deliberately do NOT do
chunks.text:
- No Presidio / no PII pipeline. The corpus is public vendor
  documentation; there is no user PII at rest. Presidio brings spaCy models
  (hundreds of MB) to solve a problem this system doesn't have yet.
  Revisit trigger: ingesting private/user-generated content.
- No IP/hostname/port redaction. They are load-bearing content in DevOps
  docs; redacting them destroys the product to protect nothing.
- No embedding-similarity attack detection. A second, fuzzier layer with
  a tunable threshold and no labeled data to tune on; the measured heuristic
  layer has to be beaten by real misses first.

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- A poisoned document is invisible to retrieval, and the ingest job stats
  say so (quarantined, quarantine_reasons) — auditable, not silent.
- Redaction runs on every chunk of every ingest (a few regexes; negligible
  vs. embedding cost).
- False negatives are possible by construction (novel phrasings); the
  red-team set is versioned and grows with every observed miss, and the
  gate keeps the measured floor from regressing.

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Addendum (2026-11-02): output handling, normalization, API controls
chunks.text:
The original decision covered what enters the corpus. Three gaps were found by testing
the system as an attacker would, not by rereading the design:

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Addendum (2026-11-02): output handling, normalization, API controls
chunks.text:
1. Output was trusted. The console rendered model Markdown as-is, so an image URL
   written by the model would be fetched by the browser with no click. A streaming
   output guard (rype_security.output_guard) now removes images, keeps links only
   to source and official-doc hosts, and redacts credentials; the renderer enforces the
   same rules again.
2. The 1.0 red-team score did not survive trivial rewrites. Character-level
   transforms of the same 15 attacks (invisible characters, look-alike letters,
   full-width forms, line splits) dropped raw recall to 0.00–0.07. Scanning normalized
   text restores 1.00 with no lost specificity
   (security-robustness-v1). Rewording and
   translation remain out of reach for regexes; that is the trigger for a learned layer.

chunks.title: ADR-0007: Layered RAG security — measured heuristics, quarantine at ingest
chunks.heading: Addendum (2026-11-02): output handling, normalization, API controls
chunks.text:
3. The ingest API was unauthenticated and fetched any URL. Ingestion now needs an
   admin key (fail closed outside dev), and URL fetches are restricted to public
   addresses on every redirect hop.

The full mapping to the OWASP LLM Top 10 lives in
docs/security/threat-model.md.

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Phase 6 calls for a LiteLLM proxy as the single entry point: routing,
fallback, caching, rate limiting, per-key budgets, cost ledger. Two of those
already exist in the thin LiteLLMClient (ADR-0004): fallback chains and
per-call cost accounting written to request_ledger. What was missing:
a response cache, and budget enforcement.

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Running the actual litellm --proxy binary was evaluated and rejected:
- It adds a container and a second configuration surface (providers, keys,
  routing) that duplicates libs/core settings — the exact drift ADR-0004's
  thin client was created to avoid.
- The machine pins litellm < 1.92 (1.92+ needs an MSVC/Rust build that
  fails here); the proxy server extra pulls a heavier dependency set that has
  not been validated under that pin.
- Its headline feature over our client — provider routing — is not yet
  needed: there is one live provider (Gemini free tier) with a fallback
  model. OpsLM routing arrives with Phase 5's served model, and is a
  one-line change to the model chain when it does.

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Implement the missing gateway concerns as a library layer,
rype_core.gateway.LLMGateway, that wraps any complete/stream client
and is dropped in where the chat service used the raw client:

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
1. Exact-match response cache (Redis). Keyed by
   sha256(model_chain + messages). A hit returns the stored answer with
   cost_usd = 0 and a … (cached) model tag, so the ledger and cost panel
   show cache hits as free — visible, not hidden. Streaming hits replay the
   stored text as a single delta then a zero-cost result, preserving the
   event shape the caller already handles.
2. Daily budget kill-switch. A Redis counter per UTC day
   (gw:spend:) accumulates real spend; when it reaches
   RYPE_GATEWAY_DAILY_BUDGET_USD the next call raises
   BudgetExceededError (surfaced as a chat error event, not a crash). The
   default ceiling is $1/day — the point is to prove the control exists on a
   free-tier stack, not to authorize spend.

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Graceful degradation is a hard requirement: every Redis operation is
wrapped so that a cache miss, a broken counter, or Redis being down entirely
falls back to a direct provider call. The gateway can slow the platform (one
Redis round-trip) but can never take it down.

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Measured (2026-07-26, demo-prep verification)
chunks.text:
Local stack, POST /v1/chat, query *"How does a Kubernetes HPA scale on custom
metrics?"*, latency_ms as reported in the done event:

Measured in two rounds on the same day (a first round, then an independent
re-verification later the same afternoon):

| | n | latency | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cache hit, round 1 | 5 | 25.0 / 29.4 / 32.4 / 33.0 ms | $0 |
| Cache hit, round 2 | 7 | 38.8 / 40.0 / 41.1 / 53.7 / 83.9 / 114.6 / 137.3 ms | $0 |
| Cache hit, all | 13 | mean 53.8 ms (gateway's own counter), range 25–137 ms | $0 |
| Cache miss (cold, upstream Gemini) | 2 | 5,290 ms and 21,085 ms | $0.0044–0.0055 |

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Measured (2026-07-26, demo-prep verification)
chunks.text:
→ roughly two orders of magnitude, occasionally three (~40×–840× across the
observed extremes). Both terms are less stable than the first round suggested.
Cold latency swings with the free-tier upstream; the hit side is not as tight
as the round-1 "25–33 ms" implied — a second round on the same machine ran
slower and wider (up to 137 ms), so that first sample was optimistic, not
representative. The honest headline is "tens of milliseconds and $0 versus
seconds and real money." The earlier "184×" figure in the README was a
fast-end case with no recorded source and is retired.

Why quote a range at all: a single multiplier here would be measurement
theatre. The number depends on an upstream we don't control, so the range is
the finding.

chunks.title: ADR-0008: LLM gateway as a library layer, not a proxy binary
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
- Repeated identical questions are instant and free; the cost panel shows a
  gemini/… (cached) row at $0 next to the paid rows — a concrete demo of
  the cache working.
- Free-tier quota is protected twice over: judged evals already cache in
  Postgres (CachedJudge), and now the chat path caches in Redis.
- Semantic (embedding-similarity) caching and per-API-key rate limiting are
  deferred: single-user demo has no key tenancy, and exact-match caching
  captures the repeated-query win without a similarity threshold to tune.
  Revisit trigger: multi-tenant deployment (keys) or measured near-duplicate
  query volume (semantic cache).
- When OpsLM is served (Phase 5/7), domain routing (ops → OpsLM, general →
  Gemini) is added to the model chain the gateway already wraps — no
  architectural change.

chunks.title: ADR-0009: Qwen3-4B + QLoRA for OpsLM
chunks.text:
Status: accepted (2026-07-18) — trained 2026-07-22 on a Colab T4 and published to
dhf1234/OpsLM-v1 (merged 16-bit + LoRA adapter + GGUF Q4_K_M); served and benchmarked
2026-07-25. The before/after-vs-base eval is still outstanding — see docs/model-registry.md.

chunks.title: ADR-0009: Qwen3-4B + QLoRA for OpsLM
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Phase 5 fine-tunes a domain model ("OpsLM") on synthetic DevOps/MLOps
instructions. The hard constraint is free GPU only (Colab/Kaggle T4,
16 GB), and the training must be resumable across Colab session limits.
Choices needed: base model, adaptation method, precision.

chunks.title: ADR-0009: Qwen3-4B + QLoRA for OpsLM
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Base model: Qwen3-4B (unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Base).
- Apache-2.0 (publishable to HF Hub without license friction).
- 4B is the quality/VRAM sweet spot: strong on technical/code text, and in
  4-bit it leaves enough T4 headroom for activations at seq-len 2048.
- Larger (7–8B) 4-bit runs are feasible on T4 but leave little margin and
  push run time past the free-session window; 1.5B trades away too much
  domain quality. 4B is the defensible middle.

Adaptation: QLoRA (4-bit NF4 base + LoRA adapters).
- LoRA r=16, alpha=16 on attention + MLP projections
  (q/k/v/o/gate/up/down) — ~0.5% of parameters trained.
- 4-bit base weights (NF4) via Unsloth keep a 4B model + optimizer state
  inside 16 GB; adamw_8bit keeps optimizer memory down further.
- Full fine-tuning and 16-bit LoRA are both out of budget on a single T4;
  QLoRA is the only method that fits with margin.

chunks.title: ADR-0009: Qwen3-4B + QLoRA for OpsLM
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text:
Tooling: Unsloth + TRL SFTTrainer.
- Unsloth ~2× throughput / lower VRAM vs stock PEFT on T4 — the difference
  between a run that finishes in a free session and one that doesn't.
- TRL SFTTrainer is the standard, and its hub_strategy="checkpoint" pushes
  every checkpoint to the Hub, giving free-session resumability
  (--resume picks up the latest).

chunks.title: ADR-0009: Qwen3-4B + QLoRA for OpsLM
chunks.heading: Training data provenance (corrected 2026-07-26)
chunks.text:
OpsLM-v1 was trained on 534 training examples — the committed
data/sft/ split: 593 pairs total, 534 train / 59 val
(data/sft/manifest.json, contaminated_dropped: 0).

The instruction generator output, data/instructions/instructions-v1.jsonl,
holds 838 examples. These two numbers are not the same thing and had been
conflated:

| Artifact | Count | Date |
|---|---|---|
| data/sft/ split — what the QLoRA run consumed | 593 (534 train / 59 val) | 2026-07-19 |
| data/instructions/instructions-v1.jsonl — generator output | 838 | scaled 2026-07-21 |

chunks.title: ADR-0009: Qwen3-4B + QLoRA for OpsLM
chunks.heading: Training data provenance (corrected 2026-07-26)
chunks.text:
The instruction set was scaled 593 → 838 on 2026-07-21, two days after the
SFT split was built and before the 2026-07-22 training run — but
prepare_sft.py was never re-run, so the extra 245 examples never reached
training. The Colab notebook clones the repo and reads data/sft/train.jsonl
directly, so the committed split is the provenance of the published
checkpoint.

The split is deliberately left as-is. Regenerating data/sft/ from the 838
file would make the committed data stop matching the published weights — the
repo would look tidier and be less true. The correct fix was to the claim, not
the data. Docs that said "fine-tuned on 838 instructions" (README, demo
runbook) now say 534 training examples.

chunks.title: ADR-0009: Qwen3-4B + QLoRA for OpsLM
chunks.heading: Training data provenance (corrected 2026-07-26)
chunks.text:
Consequence for the pending before/after eval: it grades a checkpoint
trained on 534 examples. Regenerating the split to 838 and retraining is a
