chunks.text:
Dataset: 100 questions, generated by gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite
from the ingested corpus (1241 docs /
7383 chunks; one question per document, gold label =
source chunk). Ranking depth k=10. Embeddings: BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5
(dense) + Qdrant/bm25 (sparse), reranker
BAAI/bge-reranker-base (see ADR-0003).

chunks.title: Retrieval Ablation — retrieval-v3 (2026-07-17)
chunks.heading: Reading the numbers
chunks.text:
- Chunk-level is a lower bound. The corpus contains near-duplicate content
  across documents (e.g. similar compose examples), so a retrieval that surfaces
  an equivalent-but-different chunk scores 0 at chunk level. Document-level
  credit corrects for the within-document half of that; cross-document
  duplicates still depress both.
- Latency is per query, sequential, CPU-only embeddings/rerank on the dev
  machine — comparative, not absolute.
- Raw per-case results: retrieval-ablation-v3-raw.json.

chunks.title: Retrieval Ablation — retrieval-v3 (2026-07-17)
chunks.heading: What v3 is and what it settles
chunks.text:
v3 = the 100 v2 questions paraphrased by an LLM (same meaning, different
incidental wording — mean vocabulary overlap with v2 only 0.31), gold labels
unchanged, same corpus. It exists to answer the question v2 raised: was
"sparse wins" real retrieval superiority, or vocabulary leakage from
one-question-per-chunk generation?

| chunk mrr@10 | v2 (verbatim) | v3 (paraphrased) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| dense | 0.553 | 0.570 | +0.017 |
| sparse | 0.759 | 0.611 | −0.149 |
| hybrid | 0.705 | 0.656 | −0.049 |
| hybrid+rerank | 0.745 | 0.645 | −0.100 |

chunks.title: Retrieval Ablation — retrieval-v3 (2026-07-17)
chunks.heading: What v3 is and what it settles
chunks.text:
Verdict: it was leakage, and hybrid is the right default — now with
evidence. Under paraphrase, sparse loses 20% of its MRR (its v2 win was
built on questions that reuse the gold chunk's exact tokens), dense is flat
(semantic vectors don't care about wording — its weakness is the corpus
scale, not paraphrase), and hybrid degrades 3× less than sparse because the
dense leg carries it when vocabulary shifts. Chat's default
(SearchMode.HYBRID, no rerank) stands on all three regimes: best on v1,
close second on v2, best on v3.

The honest bracketing: real user queries live somewhere between v2 (verbatim
error strings pasted into the box — sparse's home turf) and v3 (described
problems in the user's own words). Hybrid is the only mode that is
near-optimal at both ends; that is the decision rationale, not any single
table.

chunks.title: Retrieval Ablation — retrieval-v3 (2026-07-17)
chunks.heading: What v3 is and what it settles
chunks.text:
Rerank on the paraphrased set is quality-neutral-to-negative again
(0.656 → 0.645) at 10.6 s/query — the v2 "rerank helps" result does not
generalize across regimes, which reinforces keeping OPSVERSE_CHAT_RERANK
default-off.

chunks.title: Golden retrieval set v1 - pooled, graded, with uncertainty
chunks.text: Generated 2026-09-01 by opsverse_evals.golden_eval. Labels from evalsets/retrieval-golden-v1.jsonl (judge: gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite); ranked lists re-scored from the committed ablation raw JSON, so this compares labels, not runs.

chunks.title: Golden retrieval set v1 - pooled, graded, with uncertainty
chunks.heading: What changed versus the shipped eval sets
chunks.text:
retrieval-v1/v2/v3 give each question one gold label - the chunk it was generated
from. ADR-0018 showed that
makes recall@k = hit@k, precision@k = hit@k/k and contextual precision =
mrr@k. This set replaces those labels with pooled, graded judgements:

- Pooling (TREC-style): candidates pooled from dense + sparse + hybrid +
  hybrid+rerank, deduplicated - mean pool 19.14 candidates/query
  versus 10 if only one system were judged. No mode is scored solely on what it
  itself retrieved.
- Graded 0-3 (TREC convention), so nDCG can separate a full answer from an
  on-topic near-miss.
- Position-randomised: candidate order shuffled per query with a deterministic
  seed, so the judge cannot inherit any system's ranking.

chunks.title: Golden retrieval set v1 - pooled, graded, with uncertainty
chunks.heading: The labels
chunks.text:
- 100 queries, relevance threshold grade >= 2
- Relevant chunks per query: mean 3.03, range 1-13
- 70/100 queries have more than one relevant
  chunk (the whole point); 0 have none
- Grade histogram (all judgements): {0: 773, 1: 838, 2: 122, 3: 181}
- Seed recovery 100% - share of originating chunks the judge independently graded >=2. A judge-sanity check: the question was written from that chunk, so a low rate would mean the judge, not the retriever, is the problem.

chunks.title: Golden retrieval set v1 - pooled, graded, with uncertainty
chunks.heading: Did the degeneracy actually break?
chunks.text:
Re-running the ADR-0018 identity check against these labels - here a failure is the
desired result, because it means the metrics now measure different things:

- max |recall@10 - hit@10| = 0.8750
- max |ctx_precision@10 - mrr@10| = 0.7571

chunks.title: Golden retrieval set v1 - pooled, graded, with uncertainty
chunks.heading: Honest limits
chunks.text:
- The judge is a single LLM. These are LLM-graded relevance labels, not human
  ones. Seed recovery is a sanity check on the judge, not a substitute for human
  agreement; a second-annotator study is the next step, not a claim made here.
- The pool is bounded by what the four modes retrieved. A chunk no mode surfaced
  in its top-10 is unjudged and counts as irrelevant. That is the standard pooling
  assumption and it inflates recall for every system equally.
- n = 100 queries. The CIs are the honest width of that; several gaps
  below are not resolvable at this n, and are labelled so.
- Re-scored from committed ranked lists, so this isolates the effect of labels.
  It is not a fresh retrieval run.

chunks.title: Retrieval metrics audit v1 - which metrics are independent?
chunks.heading: Why this exists
chunks.text:
precision@k, recall@k and contextual precision are standard RAG-evaluation
metrics and they are now implemented in opsverse_evals.metrics. But adding them
to these eval sets would not have added information, and reporting them as if
it had would be the same mistake this project caught in ablation v2 - a number that
looks like evidence and isn't.

Every question in retrieval-v1/v2/v3 is generated from exactly one chunk, so each
query has exactly one gold label. Under that condition:


recall@k               == hit@k       (1 relevant item: you find it or you don't)
precision@k            == hit@k / k   (at most one hit in the numerator)
contextual_precision@k == mrr@k       (AP over a single relevant item = 1/rank)


The tables below verify this per case, not on the aggregate - the aggregate could
hide compensating errors.

chunks.title: Retrieval metrics audit v1 - which metrics are independent?
chunks.heading: What this means
chunks.text:
- recall@10 and hit@10 are the same column twice. precision@10 is hit@10/10.
  Quoting all three as separate evidence would inflate an evaluation suite without
  strengthening it.
- The metrics are implemented, tested and correct for the general multi-label case
  (libs/evals/tests/test_metrics_and_schemas.py pins both the identities and the
  point at which they break). They are ready for an eval set that earns them.
- To make them independent, relevance judgements must be graded over the retrieved
  candidates, not inherited from the generating chunk - that is a labelling problem,
  not a metrics problem, and it is the honest next step.

chunks.title: Retrieval metrics audit v1 - which metrics are independent?
chunks.heading: What was not done, and why
chunks.text:
Contextual recall was not implemented. Its definition requires a ground-truth
answer to attribute claims against, and this project has no reference answers: the
faithfulness judge in rag_suite.py is deliberately reference-free, grading each
claim against the retrieved context. Adding contextual recall means first writing gold
answers - real work with a real cost, not a metric to switch on.

chunks.title: Injection detector robustness v1
chunks.heading: Reading it
chunks.text:
- TPR is recall on the 15 attacks; specificity is 1 - false-positive rate on the 18
  benign sentences, which were chosen to share vocabulary with attacks.
- Attacks still missed by the normalized detector: none.
- The transforms and the normalization were written together, so this guards
  against these known tricks regressing; it is not an independent robustness test.
- n = 33 per transform. One case moves a rate by 0.07 (attacks) or 0.06 (benign),
  so treat this as a regression check, not a precise estimate.

chunks.title: Injection detector robustness v1
chunks.heading: What this does not measure
chunks.text:
Rewording, translation and encodings change the words, not the characters, and
regexes cannot be expected to catch them. Those belong to the planned learned
classifier layer (threat model T-01). A perfect score here means the character
tricks above no longer work, not that injection is detected in general.
